problems.1: Capacity and capacity in use are overconfident
problems.2: Machinery totals disagree with official statistics even though the model is pulled toward them
problems.3: Oil and gas forecasts a year ahead are far off and too confident
problems.4: Wholesale fails every check available, and one check is missing
problems.5: Inventories do not match their data
problems.6: New orders are barely determined, and often unsettled
problems.7: Ranges are too wide in most places and too narrow in a few
problems.8: Many parameters are learned only from their group
problems.10: Retail does not reproduce its own data or official sales
problems.11: The main forecast check partly grades the model against itself

fixes.label: 1A
fixes.title: Add a smaller monthly capacity revision everywhere
fixes.fix: Let every kind of business revise its capacity a little each month, but by about a quarter of the amount tried on the previous world. That earlier test raised capacity's hit rate from 74/100 to 95/100, overshooting the 90 target and widening other ranges; a smaller revision should keep most of the gain for capacity while leaving other quantities alone.
fixes.test: A four-date backtest on this world and one on another random-number set; Capacity and Capacity in use on Forecasts against later estimates should move toward 90/100 while the overall rate stays near 90-94.

fixes.label: 1B
fixes.title: Observe storage space for Wholesale and Retail
fixes.fix: Add official statistics on warehouse and store floor space so that the model sees Wholesale's and Retail's capacity directly. Capacity's misses on this world come mostly from Wholesale, whose capacity level jumps by about 40% from one as-of date to the next, and from Retail and Housing at one date each; sectors whose capacity is reported directly barely miss.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the new statistics and run a four-date backtest; Wholesale's and Retail's capacity hit rates on Forecasts against later estimates, and Capacity overall, should rise toward 90/100.

fixes.label: 1C
fixes.title: Fit capacity against official utilization too
fixes.fix: In Steel and Machinery, let the official utilization rate, not just official production, set the size of the untracked firms' capacity during fitting. Steel's production agrees with the official figure (97/100) while its utilization does not (55/100), which points to a capacity level that is off by a couple of percent rather than to output.
fixes.test: Four-date fits of Steel and Machinery on two random-number sets; their utilization rows on Sector totals against official statistics should rise above 85/100 with production staying where it is.

fixes.label: 2A
fixes.title: Size Machinery's untracked firms to official production
fixes.fix: During fitting, anchor the overall size of Machinery's untracked firms to the official production statistic. Tested alone on the previous world it took Machinery production from 0/100 to 100/100 but let finished stock go wrong at one date; now that the filter also corrects Machinery's order book month by month, the stock should have less room to drift.
fixes.test: Four-date Machinery fits on two random-number sets; Machinery production on Sector totals against official statistics should rise from 40/100 toward 90/100 and its gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall from 9.6%.

fixes.label: 2B
fixes.title: Calm the filter's Machinery order-book corrections
fixes.fix: Keep letting the filter adjust Machinery's order level, but stop it adjusting overdue orders as well, or make each adjustment smaller. Since both were added, the spread ratio for new orders has reached 11.30 (2.0 when the change was tested on the previous world) and price has become unsettled (1.72), so the corrections may be overshooting.
fixes.test: Four-date Machinery filters on two random-number sets; Machinery's new orders and price on What the data pin down should fall below 1.2 without losing its Observations against the model score.

fixes.label: 2C
fixes.title: Keep the best of three Machinery fits
fixes.fix: Fit Machinery three times at each as-of date with different random numbers, and keep the fit that best predicts observations held back from fitting. The test of the filter change found official production at 73/100 with one set of random numbers and 13/100 with another, so one unlucky fit can account for much of the disagreement.
fixes.test: Three Machinery fits per date plus a held-out check; Machinery production on Sector totals against official statistics and its Forecasts against later estimates gap should improve and vary less across dates.

fixes.label: 3A
fixes.title: Keep the best of three Oil and gas fits
fixes.fix: Fit Oil and gas three times at each as-of date with different random numbers and keep the one that best predicts observations held back from fitting. Most of the 13.6% gap comes from the 2024 run, whose order book is about four times the next run's and whose lead time is 7 to 14 months against 2 to 4 at the other dates: one fit landed far from the rest.
fixes.test: Three Oil and gas fits per date plus a held-out check, then filters; Oil and gas on Forecasts against later estimates should move from 76/100 and 13.6% toward 90/100 and under 5%.

fixes.label: 3B
fixes.title: Start Oil and gas fits from last year's answer
fixes.fix: Start each run's Oil and gas fit from the previous run's estimates instead of from the starting guesses. The 2023 and 2025 runs roughly agree while the 2024 run departs from both, and a fit that begins near last year's answer is less likely to wander off when a year of new data barely changes the picture.
fixes.test: Oil and gas fitted date by date in order, each from the previous run, then filtered; its gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall well below 13.6% and the 2024 order book and lead time should come back in line.

fixes.label: 3C
fixes.title: Loosen Oil and gas's official stock readings
fixes.fix: Give the official petroleum stock readings a larger error in fitting, or fit without them and use them only in the filter. In earlier worlds these readings drove an Oil and gas fit to blow up at the 2024 date, and here Oil and gas's finished inventory is unsettled (1.57) and differs fiftyfold between runs.
fixes.test: Four-date Oil and gas fits with the readings loosened and without them; Oil and gas on Forecasts against later estimates and its finished inventory on What the data pin down should improve without hurting its official-statistic agreement.

fixes.label: 4A
fixes.title: Anchor Wholesale's untracked stock to sector inventories
fixes.fix: During fitting, tie the stock held by Wholesale's untracked firms to the whole-sector inventory statistic, as Machinery's size can be tied to official production. Those firms hold most of the sector's stock and no other reading reaches them; the sector inventory readings now miss 96 months in 100, although they fit 93-97/100 when the price index was tested on the previous world.
fixes.test: Four-date Wholesale fits on two random-number sets; Sector inventories and Wholesale on Observations against the model should rise from 4/100 and 67/100 toward 90/100.

fixes.label: 4B
fixes.title: Keep the best of three Wholesale fits
fixes.fix: Fit Wholesale three times at each as-of date with different random numbers and keep the fit that best predicts held-back observations. Wholesale's capacity level moves by about 40% between runs, up at one date and down at the next, which looks like fits landing in different places rather than real change. This differs from an earlier, untested idea of pooling all three fits into one forecast.
fixes.test: Three Wholesale fits per date plus a held-out check, then filters; Wholesale on Forecasts against later estimates should rise from 81/100 and its capacity and utilization should stop jumping between runs.

fixes.label: 4C
fixes.title: Check Wholesale against official wholesale sales
fixes.fix: Add the official monthly wholesale sales figure to the comparison with official statistics, without letting the filter pull toward it. Used as an input to fitting on an earlier world it made things worse, but as a check only it gives Wholesale the outside test it now lacks.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the sales figure and filter Wholesale at four dates; Sector totals against official statistics should show a Wholesale row, and it should agree if the other fixes work.

fixes.label: 4D
fixes.title: Find what clashes with the new price index
fixes.fix: Run Wholesale's filter at each date with and without the new official price index. If the sector inventory readings fit again without it, let the model estimate how far the index can stray from Wholesale's own average price instead of trusting it as given, so the index stops forcing a price level the other data reject.
fixes.test: Wholesale filters at four dates with and without the index, then a refit with the index's error estimated; Sector inventories should rise from 4/100 while Wholesale's Forecasts against later estimates gap stays near 4.5% or better.

fixes.label: 5A
fixes.title: Add materials inventories in four sectors only
fixes.fix: Add official monthly materials inventories for Food, Chemicals, Steel and Autos, the four sectors where an earlier test pinned input inventory (spread ratios 0.18-0.76 from about 1), and leave out Oil and gas and Housing, where it did not help and an Oil and gas fit blew up. Give the readings a somewhat larger error so they do not pull other quantities off.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world, run a four-date backtest on two random-number sets; input inventory's spread ratio on What the data pin down should fall below 0.8 in those four sectors with no sector getting worse elsewhere.

fixes.label: 5B
fixes.title: Give each firm its own normal stock level
fixes.fix: Let each firm have its own normal stock level, pulled toward the sector's, instead of one level for the whole sector. The filter keeps pulling every firm's stock back toward the shared level, so firms that hold more or less stock than that drift away from their own reports; company inventory reports are inside their ranges only 71 months in 100.
fixes.test: Four-date backtests on two random-number sets; Finished inventory on Observations against the model should rise from 71/100 toward 90/100.

fixes.label: 5C
fixes.title: Let stocked-out copies recover their inventory
fixes.fix: Remove the filter rule that stops adjusting a simulated copy's finished stock for good once that copy has run out with orders late. A copy that runs out early can then never be brought back to what the inventory readings say, which would show as readings missed by a wide margin.
fixes.test: A four-date backtest; Finished inventory and Sector inventories on Observations against the model should rise, and finished inventory spread ratios should fall below 1.

fixes.label: 6A
fixes.title: Use a filter update that cannot widen
fixes.fix: Replace the filter's random perturbation of observations with a deterministic version of the same update, which by its nature can only narrow the copies' spread. Spread ratios above 1 for new orders in six sectors mean that adding data makes the copies disagree more, and with 100 copies the random noise added to each reading can do exactly that for quantities the readings barely touch.
fixes.test: Four-date backtests on two random-number sets; new orders' spread ratios on What the data pin down should fall to 1 or below in all sectors, with Observations against the model no worse.

fixes.label: 6B
fixes.title: Measure spread over the whole history
fixes.fix: Compute the spread ratio from the copies' total spread over the history, with and without data, instead of averaging month-by-month ratios, and report the months where single copies ran away. An earlier test cut the quantities above 1.2 from 13-18 per date to 7-13 and found runaway copies behind several; this time adopt it and list runaway months beside the ratio so readers can tell real conflict from a few wild copies.
fixes.test: Recompute What the data pin down from this world's runs; the number of sectors with new orders above 1.2 should fall from six, and the rest should name the runaway months.

fixes.label: 7A
fixes.title: Recalibrate the widening on newer worlds
fixes.fix: Reset the single factor that widens every forecast range, using backtests of the current model on the two or three newest synthetic worlds instead of the older world it was set on. Several changes since then, including the stricter treatment of official statistics and the filter's order-book corrections, have made the model's own ranges wider, so nine sectors now come out wider than needed.
fixes.test: Four-date backtests of the current model on two earlier worlds to set the factor, then this world's ranges rebuilt; the overall rate on Forecasts against later estimates should fall from 94/100 toward 90/100, with Oil and gas and Wholesale watched.

fixes.label: 7B
fixes.title: Widen each sector by how much its fits wander
fixes.fix: Refit every sector with a second set of random numbers at each date and set each sector's widening from how far its two fits disagree, rather than one factor for all. The too-narrow sectors, Oil and gas and Wholesale, are exactly those where fits land far apart from run to run, while stable sectors such as Hotels and Airlines would get narrower ranges.
fixes.test: A second four-date backtest with other random numbers, then ranges rebuilt; on Forecasts against later estimates the spread of sector hit rates should narrow toward 85-95/100.

fixes.label: 7C
fixes.title: Pool three fits into each forecast
fixes.fix: Combine three fits per run, each with different random numbers, into one set of copies, and lower the widening factor accordingly. Ranges would then carry the uncertainty that comes from the fit itself, which is large in Oil and gas, Wholesale and Machinery and small elsewhere, instead of applying one fixed stretch everywhere.
fixes.test: Three four-date backtests pooled, widening refit; sector hit rates on Forecasts against later estimates should move toward 90/100 from both sides.

fixes.label: 8A
fixes.title: Add gross margins to company reports
fixes.fix: Add the cost of goods sold, or gross margin, to tracked companies' quarterly reports. Today nothing measures a firm's unit cost directly, so its cost pass-through and normal markup can only be guessed from price and revenue; by the stricter measure they are learned for about one entity in six.
fixes.test: Rebuild the world with the new figures and run a four-date backtest; the share of pass-through and markup informative by the stricter ratio on What the data pin down should rise well above 20 of 115.

fixes.label: 8B
fixes.title: Share pass-through and markup where data are thin
fixes.fix: In sectors where observations held back from fitting are predicted as well or better, use one pass-through and one markup for the whole sector instead of one per firm. An earlier test of this for other parameters (capacity drift, emissions slope, list-price gap) only flattered the count and made accuracy worse, so this is worth trying only for these two, which are the least learned, and only with the held-out check deciding.
fixes.test: A held-out check per sector to choose, then a four-date backtest; the stricter informative share on What the data pin down should rise with Observations against the model no worse.

fixes.label: 9A
fixes.title: Mark negligible quantities instead of dividing
fixes.fix: Where a quantity is almost always zero, as lost demand is in Hospitals, Hotels and Airlines, report it as negligible rather than as a ratio of two tiny spreads, and measure the rest from total spread over the history. In those sectors the forecast range for lost demand is often exactly zero wide, so a single wild copy can make the ratio look like 216.
fixes.test: Recompute What the data pin down from this world's runs; Hospitals', Hotels' and Airlines' lost demand should no longer be listed as unsettled.

fixes.label: 9B
fixes.title: Stop copies running away in service sectors
fixes.fix: In Hotels, Hospitals and Airlines, limit how far one filter update can push a copy's demand above what it can serve. An earlier investigation found that after a hotel lost capacity, one update pushed every copy's demand above its output and left them stuck there, and an earlier test traced the large lost-demand ratios in Hospitals and Hotels to such runaway copies.
fixes.test: Four-date filters of the three service sectors on two random-number sets; their lost-demand spread ratios on What the data pin down should fall below 1.2.

fixes.label: 9C
fixes.title: Record advance bookings in the month observed
fixes.fix: In the service sectors only, write the filter's correction to advance bookings into the month that was observed, not the month after. An earlier investigation found this made Hotels' readings far more likely under the true numbers, but it was not adopted because it changed every sector's filter; limiting it to Hotels, Hospitals and Airlines avoids that.
fixes.test: Four-date filters of the three service sectors; lost demand on What the data pin down should settle and their Observations against the model scores should hold.

fixes.label: 10A
fixes.title: Check how Retail sales are compared
fixes.fix: Check step by step how the model's Retail sales value is compared with the official retail sales figure: which price turns volume into dollars, whether lost sales are counted, and the base of the price index. The gap is 3.3% on this world and also on the previous one with different random numbers, while most official statistics sit under 1%, which points to a steady mismatch rather than bad luck.
fixes.test: Fix any mismatch found and rerun Retail at four dates; retail sales on Sector totals against official statistics should rise from 83/100 with the gap well under 3.3%.

fixes.label: 10B
fixes.title: Use a filter update that cannot widen, in Retail
fixes.fix: Try the deterministic version of the filter update in Retail alone, where it is cheapest to test. An earlier test found Retail's copies really do spread about three times wider with data, with no runaway copies, which points at the filter's random perturbation of readings rather than at the measure.
fixes.test: Four-date Retail filters on two random-number sets; Retail's order book, new orders, shipments and load factor on What the data pin down should fall to 1 or below and Observations against the model should rise from 88/100.

fixes.label: 10C
fixes.title: Limit what Retail's sector totals can move
fixes.fix: Let the official retail statistics update only the quantities they measure and their direct inputs, not every hidden quantity of every store. With 100 copies, chance links between a sector total and an unrelated quantity, such as one store's lost demand, can push copies apart instead of together.
fixes.test: Four-date Retail filters; Retail's unsettled quantities on What the data pin down should fall below 1.2 with retail sales agreement no worse.

fixes.label: 11A
fixes.title: Check forecasts against later observations
fixes.fix: Add a check of each forecast against the observations that arrived after its as-of date, which does not involve the model's own later estimate at all. It would show whether forecasts of quantities the model mostly invents, such as input inventory, hold up against real readings, and separate accuracy from mere consistency.
fixes.test: Compute the new check from this world's four runs; it should give hit rates and gaps by sector that differ from Forecasts against later estimates where the model grades itself.

fixes.label: 11B
fixes.title: Show data-informed and model-only scores side by side
fixes.fix: On Forecasts against later estimates, show the hit rate and gap separately for values informed by data and values that come mostly from the model, rather than dropping the latter. An earlier test that dropped them moved the overall rate only from 94/100 to 93/100 and found that lead time and order book are too wide even when data-informed, so showing both makes clear which scores rest on the model alone.
fixes.test: Rebuild the page from this world's runs; input inventory and similar quantities should appear only in the model-only column.
